text: The walking and the climbing are cleanly separated here and the boundary is a flat spot, but the climb does not start above camp — it starts several hundred feet below it and on the far side of the ridge, and that is what parties get wrong. Follow the crest south from the saddle beside Observation Rock until the ridge stops rising and levels out at about 10,200 to 10,300 ft. You will know the place without being told, because four things sit together there and nowhere else: room for a couple of small tents on flat ground, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon Glacier immediately east of you, huge banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and a clean view straight across at Liberty Ridge. From that camp the route drops west off the crest a few hundred feet onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, aiming for a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the middle of the face. Look that crossing over from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there and its condition changes year to year. The traverse down to it passes under the run-out of the ice cliffs and is usually walked across old avalanche debris and stray boulders sitting on the ice, so it is done in the dark and fast. Two ways to know you are wrong. If you have descended onto the Mowich Glacier and kept going west or south, you are wandering out onto Mowich Face ground rather than to the schrund. And if you cross a bergschrund with no ice cliffs above and to your left, stop: from the schrund the route rises back east, climber's left, toward those cliffs, not away from them. The route finishes on Liberty Cap; Columbia Crest is a separate trip across the summit plateau and is not part of this climb.
runs: a bridge just left of a rock outcropping

text: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.
runs: to curtis ridge where there are good bivy sites
of the ice cliffs where the russell calves onto

text: The historic Lithuanian Lip: go up and out the roof, get over the top, then aid a bolt ladder (or free climb it at 5.13- for strong parties) to a bolted belay. Most parties aid this section for the route's standard 5.11a grade.
runs: lithuanian lip go up and out the roof

text: A long, excellent pitch up a left-facing corner and slab with beautiful moments of exposure over the East Face; belay off a large tree.
runs: long excellent pitch up a left facing corner and slab with

text: Reached by traversing climber's left along the third-class ledges at the top of the route, or by downclimbing the last pitch of the Beckey Route. The anchor is shiny bolts with chains set in a corner or shallow alcove on a steep wall overlooking the Liberty Bell-Concord notch — you have to look down over the edge a little to see it, and it is not visible from the ledge above.
runs: on a steep wall overlooking the liberty bell concord

text: Follows Liberty Crack's original aid line but climbed entirely free; pitch 1 (5.11-) leads to the crux pitch 2 'Lithuanian Lip' (5.13b) - a scrunchy, powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip and committing moves to a small stance. A slab variation on pitch 3 (5.12) avoids the original bolt ladder.
runs: powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip

text: The Lithuanian Lip, free: fun 5.11- corner climbing leads to a scrunchy, powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip; lock in, high-step to the lip, and stick 5.12- moves to a small stance below the old bolt ladder. This is the pitch Brooke Sandahl first led on gear in 1991.
runs: powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip lock

text: Grade V alpine, 5.9 YDS, 26 pitches, approximately 2,000 ft (606 m) of climbing. Route composition: Beckey Route on Liberty Bell (5.3-5.6), North Face of Concord Tower, North Face of Lexington Tower, Northwest Corner of North Early Winter Spire (5.9+), Southwest Rib of South Early Winter Spire. Hazards include significant rockfall danger in the approach gully, which funnels falling rock like a bowling alley, exposed alpine terrain, route finding challenges. Requires excellent trad climbing skills, solid alpine rock climbing experience, and good protection/anchor placement ability. Standard rack with couple bigger pieces for North Early Winter Spire. Short rappel descent from summits. The individual summits, the Beckey Route above all, are busy on summer weekends, though few parties do the full traverse. Best season: July-August during optimal weather windows. Typically done as 1-2 day alpine climb with experienced parties.
runs: couple bigger pieces for north early winter spire

text: Descend the southwest face route: roughly 2,000 ft of steep snow and ice up to 65°, downclimbed in good conditions and otherwise rappelled. Below the face, traverse back along the north side of the peak toward Heliotrope Ridge, roped for the glacier, and walk out the Heliotrope Ridge Trail.
runs: back along the north side of the peak

text: From Mount Baker Highway (SR-542) about 1 mile past the Glacier Public Service Center, turn right onto Glacier Creek Road (FR-39), follow it about 8 miles, then turn left at the junction and go less than half a mile to the trailhead.
runs: less than half a mile to the trailhead
mile past the glacier public service center turn right onto

text:
The highest trees in the basin are the camp, and the camp is the last thing you can navigate to. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

The bergschrund is the base of the climb. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

Do not expect one clean couloir — this is the trap the name sets. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the highest notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

The serac step is the confirmation. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

And the aspect settles the coarse error: this route faces southwest and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.
runs: narrow chute and trends right out of view

text: Ascend steep snow from the center of the Green Creek Glacier and cross a potentially tricky moat/bergschrund to gain the center or right side of the 500-ft-wide face. Climb sustained, moderate 5.4 face climbing on solid rock for roughly 600 ft (4 pitches), then continue over easier, looser terrain — the full wall, including this upper scrambling, is nearly 1,000 ft top to bottom.
runs: gain the center or right side of the

text: Cross the moat/bergschrund and gain moderate-angle rock on the center or right side of the face.
runs: the center or right side of the face

text: From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road), the Elbow Lake Trail reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack River within a few minutes. The bridge is gone and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible during high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently in place. One group used a log crossing roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction; another used an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it, and treat the crossing as the crux of the day in terms of consequence. Once across, follow the Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old-growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback (near Hildebrand Creek), find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off and heading up the Green Creek drainage. It is marked with small blue diamond trail markers. Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, then up through the brush-filled Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. The Green Glacier approach is 5 miles one way with 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead over trail, climbers' trail, boulder fields, scree and slabs. For the South Couloir specifically, continue up the basin and climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of Little Sister, then traverse onto the south side and up into the gully. In deep winter one party found hard snow all the way to the col; snowshoes were left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
runs: there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and

text: From the Mt. Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on Highway 9 to Acme. About 7.2-7.6 miles past the office, after crossing the South Fork Nooksack River, turn right on Mosquito Lake Road and follow it roughly 9 miles. After crossing the Middle Fork Nooksack River, turn right onto Forest Road 38 and drive about 11-12 miles to the Elbow Lake Trailhead on the right, with parking directly across the road. FR 38 is dirt and subject to washouts. Coming from Bellingham, reach Mosquito Lake Road via Highway 542 through Deming. Note that despite the 'Mt Baker Hwy' area label, SR 542 is not the access road for this peak.
runs: nooksack river turn right on mosquito lake road and follow it

text: Begin at the col between Cinderella and Little Sister. Closely follow the jagged ridgeline on easy but exposed low-5th-class climbing on great rock, then pick a way through looser, broader 4th-class terrain on the upper mountain to the true summit.
runs: easy but exposed low 5th class climbing on great rock

text: Downclimb the route, or rappel the North Face on scattered tat and pin anchors.
runs: downclimb the route or rappel the north face on scattered tat and pin anchors

text: Light alpine rack; tat for anchors if rappelling the North Face option instead of downclimbing.
runs: light alpine rack tat for anchors if rappelling

text: Leave the Wonderland Trail and climb steep talus/heather slopes to gain the lower edge of the Fryingpan Glacier; route-finding through boulders, often snow-covered into midsummer.
runs: to gain the lower edge of the fryingpan glacier

text: The obvious low point in the ridge just left of Little Tahoma; cross here from the Fryingpan Glacier onto the Whitman Glacier.
runs: in the ridge just left of little tahoma

text: Scramble across a tiny notch and up the final face, Class 3 to 4 on rotten andesite, then along the narrow crest to the summit at 11,138 ft. Many parties rope up; the crest drops about 2,000 ft to the Emmons Glacier on the north side.
runs: scramble across a tiny notch and up the

text: Keep the group tight, avoid stacking multiple parties on the loose rock, and never linger directly below other climbers.
runs: parties on the loose rock and never linger

text: Early July into early August is the genuinely optimal window: the Fryingpan/Whitman glaciers are still well filled and crevasses well-bridged, and the loose summit block is more often frozen solid on an early-morning ascent. By late August-September the glaciers melt out, crevasse bridges weaken, and rockfall increases markedly as the ice holding the andesite together recedes.
runs: bridges weaken and rockfall increases markedly as the

text: A short, exposed scramble across a tiny notch and up the final face to the summit (11,138 ft), graded Class 3 to 4; many parties rope up. The east ridge is a narrow fin of rotten andesite dropping about 2,000 ft to the Emmons Glacier on the north. There are two lines up the final step; old anchors may be found, and some parties use them for a short rappel on the way down.
runs: scramble across a tiny notch and up the

text: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
runs: the crest between the fryingpan and whitman glaciers

text:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
runs: its upper left hand corner into a gully

text: Live Free or Die climbs the East Face for 8 pitches to M&M Ledge (roughly mid-height), then shares its final 3-4 pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead take Thin Red Line’s rappel line: from M&M Ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber’s left to bolted anchors and make four more double-rope rappels to the talus at the base of the East Face.
runs: with the upper section of thin red line
downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem

text:
Same East Face approach as Liberty Crack: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face.

Eleven pitches, climbed in 2017. The route takes the East Face for eight pitches to M&M Ledge at roughly mid-height, then shares its final three or four pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line.
runs: with the upper section of thin red line

text:
The route is sandwiched, and the sandwich is the test: it lies to the left of the Independence Route and to the right of Thin Red Line. Those two neighbours are the most identifiable lines at that end of the face, so bound the ground between them and the route is inside it.

The right-hand bound is the one you can see from furthest away: the Independence Route starts at the far right, or north, edge of the East Face, and a red-coloured roof and alcove, the Baer Ceiling, sits about 85 m above its start. If a red roof is above you, you have walked one route too far right.

The left-hand bound: Thin Red Line is climber's right of Liberty Crack, and Liberty and Injustice for All sits about 10 m right of Thin Red Line on two-bolt anchors with fixed biners. If you are at a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners a rope length up, you started too far left.

An honest warning from the first ascent, and it changes how you read the wall: the party recorded that the route's initial crack pitches were 700 ft up the wall and seemed to have been reached by rappel from other routes, with no obvious way to reach them from below. So the visible feature that names this route is not at its base. Do not try to identify the line by the cracks; identify the ground between Thin Red Line and Independence and start there.

Descent from M&M ledge, for parties who do not top out, is Thin Red Line's: from the ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber's-left to a set of bolted anchors and make four double-rope rappels back to the talus at the base of the East Face. Every station after the first is bolted; no natural or v-thread anchors are involved. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent on the west side instead.
runs: up the wall and seemed to have been reached by rappel from other routes
no obvious way to reach them from below

text: Climb the glacier to the low gap west of Spider Mountain, then descend steep snow and scree on the far side to the tarns. In whiteout this is easy ground to get wrong — the gap is the only obvious break in the ridge.
runs: glacier to the low gap west of spider mountain

text: Leave I-90 at Exit 54 (Hyak) and follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, staying on it past the end of the pavement for about 5.4 miles to the Ollallie Meadow junction where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and keep driving until the road ends in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin; that turnaround is where you park, and the pin here marks the PCT crossing rather than the road end itself. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from about July through November.
runs: ends in a large turnaround just below silver basin

text: A standard sport rack of quickdraws sized for a 2-pitch bolted line; bring enough draws to cover the longer pitch plus the anchor. Bolted chain anchors at the top of each pitch allow rappelling or lowering — no trad gear is needed for protection.
runs: chain anchors at the top of each pitch

text: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
runs: a red talus gully east of the carru lago saddle

text: Rope up at the col and make a rising traverse across the upper Richardson Glacier to Luahna's East Ridge near 8,000 ft, then scramble the ridge west to the summit. A short, steep step low on the ridge goes at about low Class 4; ledges and a parallel gully to one side get around it.
runs: a rising traverse across the upper richardson glacier to

text: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, at the end of White River Road/FR 6400, reached via WA-207 and White River Road from Coles Corner off US-2), follow the White River Trail (#1507) upstream along a mostly level grade through old-growth forest for about 4 miles to its junction with the Boulder Pass Trail (#1562, also called the Boulder Creek Trail). Water is abundant the whole way — the White River parallels the trail, and Boulder Creek is a dependable source at the junction (the crossing here can be a ford depending on the year/season, so check recent trip reports before committing). Turn onto the Boulder Pass Trail and climb switchbacks through forest, gaining roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about 3 miles to break out into the open basin below Boulder Pass (~5,000 ft). Because the round trip from the trailhead runs in the 20+ mile range with well over 6,000 ft of gain, most parties do this as an overnight, camping in the Boulder Pass basin or pushing on to a high camp in Upper Boulder Basin (~5,800 ft). From the basin, leave the maintained trail for the unmaintained 'sheepherder's path,' a boot track that sidehills west across a series of cirques (Clark Basin, then Luahna Basin), losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining elevation near a 7,200 ft spur. This traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or snow cover. From the spur, a rising traverse across broad benches (often snow-covered well into summer) and easy Class 2 ledges leads to the ~7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain; from there a rising traverse across the upper Richardson Glacier (real crevasse hazard — carry glacier travel gear, and note the glacier has been reported thinning/broken-up and less straightforward in recent years) reaches Luahna's East Ridge, which is scrambled west to the summit.
runs: a rising traverse across the upper richardson glacier

text: Real hazard — the standard line from the 7,600 ft col makes a rising traverse across the upper Richardson Glacier with real crevasse hazard (carry glacier travel gear); parties can avoid this by staying on rock via the south/southeast ridge instead in low-snow years.
runs: a rising traverse across the upper richardson glacier

text:
The arrival at the climbing is a glacier, and the thing that gets you to it is a col that belongs to the next peak. From the 7,200 ft spur, make a rising traverse across broad benches — often snow-covered well into summer — and easy Class 2 ledges to the roughly 7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain. You are navigating to a gap beside a different summit, which is what makes it findable: Clark is the big thing on your left.

From that col, the route is one rising traverse across the Upper Richardson Glacier to Luahna's east ridge. Rope up at the col. The glacier crossing is the route; the ridge above it is a scramble west to the summit.

The critical negative marker is about which glacier you are on: the Pilz and Butterfly Glaciers are on Luahna's north slope and belong to a separate route approached from the Napeequa side. This route uses the Richardson, which lies to the south-east of the summit. If the glacier you have stepped onto is north of the peak, you are on the other mountain's business entirely.

The second negative marker is simpler: if you never touched a glacier at all, you are on the south-west slopes and south-east ridge line, which is the other route on this peak and is deliberately glacier-free. Both finish on the same summit and neither is a variation of the other.

Coming down, the one piece of technical ground is below the east ridge: a short, steep step reported as low Class 4 and sometimes verglassed in an adjacent gully. Strong parties downclimb it; a single 20-30 m rappel off a horn or block is common practice when it is wet or icy. There is no fixed anchor — carry webbing.

Do not take the thunder creek exit on the strength of the map. Dropping south into Thunder Creek looks shorter and is reported slower and rougher, with heavy blowdown, avalanche debris and a boot path that disappears near the creek crossing. Reversing the ascent line over Boulder Pass is the reliable way out.
runs: rising traverse across the upper richardson glacier to

text: A rising traverse across the upper Richardson Glacier reaches Luahna's East Ridge. Real crevasse hazard — carry glacier travel gear; the glacier has been reported thinning/broken-up and less straightforward in recent years.
runs: a rising traverse across the upper richardson glacier

text: Follow the White River Trail and Boulder Creek Trail #1562 to the ford camp near 3,700 ft and on up to a high camp in upper Boulder Basin near 5,800 ft. From camp follow the faint sheepherder's path across Clark Basin and Luahna Basin, make a rising traverse toward the roughly 7,500 ft ridge point, and follow a faint trail across scree above Chalangin Basin to the base. Climb Class 2 ledges on the south face to the right-hand skyline ridge, cross the exposed Class 3+ traverse on the north side beneath the summit, and finish with Class 3 straight up.
runs: class 2 ledges on the south face to the

text:
You find the base of this route by counting basins, and the answer is four. From the Boulder Basin camp the sheepherder's path crosses cirques in order: boulder, then Clark, then Luahna, and the peak's base sits above the fourth — Chalangin Basin. Nothing about the ground tells you which cirque you are in, but the character does: the first is where the path keeps disappearing, the second is open and park-like, the third has good tread. Count them.

The intermediate marker is a number on the ridge: make a rising traverse across Luahna Basin toward the roughly 7,500 ft ridge point, then follow a faint trail across scree and talus above the fourth cirque to the peak's base. Above Chalangin Basin, not in it.

The positive test at the base is the grade, and it is easier than you expect: the scramble begins on easy class 2 ledges on the south face, leading up to the right-hand skyline ridge. Class 2 ledges, south-facing, and a ridge on your right at the top of them. If your first ground is steep, or if you are on a glacier, or if the ledges lead left, you are not on it.

The confirmation comes high and it is on the wrong side of the mountain: just beneath the summit the route crosses an exposed class 3+ traverse on the north side before the final Class 3 scramble straight up. So the sequence is south-face ledges, gain the ridge, cross to the north beneath the summit, then straight up. A route that never leaves the sunny side has not reached the summit block.

The negative marker against the peak's other route: the east slopes line crosses the upper Richardson Glacier from a col west of Clark Mountain and needs glacier gear. This route touches no glacier at all. If you are roping up for crevasses, you are on the other one, and it is a different day.

A note on what is published versus what parties find: this is described as a second-class line, and most parties meet a short Class 3 or better traverse or step to bypass a gap in the ridge below the true summit. Expect it rather than treat it as evidence you are off route.
runs: across scree and talus above the fourth cirque
easy class 2 ledges on the south face

text:
The route is the glacier immediately south of the peak, and the test is that it narrows. From the floor of Luna Cirque, get onto the hanging glacier that lies directly south of Phantom and follow it up to where it narrows and steepens as it flows down from higher on the mountain. That constriction is the route; there is nothing subtle about walking into a narrowing throat of ice with rock on both sides.

Arrival at the rock, which is the actual base of the climbing: where the narrows end, turn north and climb over a rock step to reach the highest snowfield on the peak. That turn is the transition from snow to rock and the point at which the party commits to the upper route. The whole climb above the cirque is only about 400 ft in four pitches, so if you have been climbing rock for more than a few rope lengths without reaching a summit block you are not on this line.

Countable confirmation: one rock step, two to three pitches of easy slab to the ridge, then a summit block of about 25 ft. Four pitches, 4th class with a move of easy 5th. Parties carry runners and a few pieces rather than a full rack, because placements on the slab are where the features allow rather than where you want them.

The turnaround test, which is the most useful thing about this route: the hanging glacier has to be recrossed to get home. A party that finds it in poor condition on the way up should treat that as the turnaround decision rather than pressing on. Timing is the main decision this route asks of a party, and the answer is taken at the base, not at the top.
runs: turn north and climb over a rock step to

text: Where the narrows end, turn north and climb over a rock step to reach the highest snowfield on the peak. This is the transition from snow to rock and the point at which the party commits to the upper route; the whole climb above the cirque is only about 400 ft in four pitches, so the step is short, but it is what stands between the glacier and the upper mountain.
runs: turn north and climb over a rock step to

text: The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR 20 (North Cascades Highway, ~2,050ft), where parking is right off the highway. From there it's about a 0.8-mile hike down the Ross Dam Trail to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a paddled canoe/packraft for parties without a shuttle reservation) roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead (~1,600ft) near the Big Beaver / 39 Mile camp area — this lake crossing is a key logistical step, not an afterthought, since Ross Lake Resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can actually reach the trailhead. From the Big Beaver Trailhead, follow the Big Beaver Trail through old-growth cedar forest along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek for about 8 miles to Luna Camp (an established backcountry campsite, permit required from the NPS backcountry office), gaining only modest elevation on generally mellow, well-graded tread. Continue north on the Big Beaver Trail roughly 1.5 more miles past Luna Camp; watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek (~2,460ft) — this is the turn onto the Access Creek approach. Ford Big Beaver Creek here (can run high with snowmelt in early season) and pick up the boot path along the north flank of Access Creek through semi-open forest. Around 3,700ft the brush thickens substantially; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint climbers' path use talus benches to avoid the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This creek-drainage stretch is the approach crux: expect sustained bushwhacking, blowdown, and route-finding, and budget real time for it. The path deposits you in the open upper basin at the Access Creek headwaters (~4,400ft), a common base-camp location roughly 1,700ft above Luna Camp. From camp, ascend broad talus (snow-filled early season) gullies southwest toward an obvious gap in the ridge above; once on the ridge, traverse south of Point 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's SE side, then cross that basin at about the 6,600ft level to Luna Col (7,200ft), the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. There is no reliable water above Access Creek camp except lingering snowmelt, so tank up before the final push.

text:
The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at about 2,050 ft, with parking right off the highway. About 0.8 mile of trail leads down to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft. The lake crossing is a logistical step rather than an afterthought, since the resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can reach the trailhead at all.

From the Big Beaver Trailhead, about 8 miles of well-graded trail through old-growth cedar along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek reach Luna Camp. Continue roughly 1.5 miles past it and watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek at about 2,460 ft. Ford Big Beaver Creek there.

Around 3,700 ft the brush thickens; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint path use talus benches to dodge the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This stretch is the approach crux. The path deposits you in the open basin at the Access Creek headwaters at about 4,400 ft, the common base camp.
runs: just north of where access creek enters big beaver creek

text:
This route contours where the south ridge climbs, and the difference starts above camp rather than at the col. From the Access Creek basin, ascend broad talus gullies, snow-filled early season, southwest toward an obvious gap in the ridge above. Once on the ridge, traverse south of point 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's southeast side, then cross that basin at about the 6,600 ft level to Luna Col at 7,200 ft.

So the fog test is an altimeter test: the basin crossing is held at roughly 6,600 ft. Losing height into the basin or gaining it toward the crest both cost you, and both are what happens when you navigate by feel. Hold the contour and it delivers you to the col.

Arrival: Luna Col at 7,200 ft is the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. You are there when the ground drops away on the far side.

Confirm on the climb, and the count is short: above the col the route is roughly 1,100 ft of class 2-3 talus and scree to the false, southern summit, then one short connecting ridge to the true summit. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left at the false summit.

The one technical spot, and its tell: drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit onto a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest with a snow-covered cliff falling several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff dropping the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the worst of it by dropping onto a ledge on the southeast side and scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit. If you are on a crest with snow on your left and bare rock on your right, you are in the right place and there is one short section of it.

No water above the access creek basin. The summit push is done on what you carry.
runs: once on the ridge traverse south of point 6 730 on grass and heather

text: Most parties reverse the West Ridge: from the true (west) summit, downclimb the class 3-4 ridge crest back toward the notch/saddle used on the way up, staying on the north side of the crest per the standard line and reversing the short crux step (a ~6 ft downclimb at a minor notch). Many parties downclimb this cleanly, but a single short rappel (roughly 15 m/50 ft, well within a 30 m single-rope length) is commonly used here instead, especially in wet conditions or with less experienced climbers — anchors are natural (slung horns/blocks or a small nut/cam placement backed by a cordelette), not bolted; there's no fixed hardware on this route. From the saddle, either reverse the ascent couloir into Lundin Basin (a fast glissade of up to 1,200-1,500 ft when it's still snow-filled, typically only reliable early season) or walk scree/talus down toward the Red-Lundin col to pick up the use trail back into Commonwealth Basin and the PCT. An alternative some parties use is descending the East Ridge instead: scramble down the crest about 100 ft to the top of a small cliff band, then make one single-rope rappel (30 m is sufficient; natural tree/horn anchors — the ridge has plenty of trees to sling) down to easy ledges, continuing to a notch in the ridge crest from which an early-season glissade or scramble rejoins the standard route in Lundin/Commonwealth Basin. This option requires either looping back on foot into Commonwealth Basin or a car shuttle/hitch between the Alpental and PCT-North trailheads, since the two approaches start at different lots. Bottom line for planning: expect zero to one short rappel (under 15 m, single rope, natural gear anchors — no bolts) — conditions and party comfort level determine whether it's downclimbed or rapped. Total descent to the trailhead runs roughly 2-2.5 hours.
runs: 100 ft to the top of a small cliff

text: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), about 23.1 miles of gravel road from Marblemount, at roughly 3,600 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here. Overnight parties also need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit for Kool-Aid Lake, picked up in person in Marblemount before you drive out.

text: Descent reverses the ascent line down the South Ridge. From the true summit (7,610 ft), climb back down the Class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew the east side of the summit tower, then climb back up the roughly 80 ft dirty gully to the false summit (about 300 ft southeast of the true summit) before continuing down the easy heather/scree of the South Ridge to the Magic Mountain-Hurry Up col. This corkscrew section is the technical crux of the whole outing — loose, broken rock with real exposure — and is where the route's single rappel comes in: many parties downclimb it as Class 3-4 with a spotting belay, but a short single-rope rappel (roughly 50-80 ft, well within a 30m or 60m single strand, or a doubled 30m rope) off a natural anchor — a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there are no bolts or fixed hardware reported on this remote, lightly-traveled summit — is commonly used by parties wanting to avoid down-climbing the loose ledges, especially in wet or snowy conditions. From the col, retrace the approach: down to Kool-Aid Lake, back up and over Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier snow slopes and the Mixup Peak traverse to Cascade Pass, then out the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock on the corkscrew ledges and the upper gully, and for soft/rotten snow on the Cache Glacier descent later in the day — this is a route best started early to avoid downclimbing softened snow on the return.

text:
The bergschrund is the route's identity and it is the one-look test against both its neighbours on this side of the mountain. This is the only Magic Mountain route from the Kool-Aid Lake side that crosses a schrund. The Northwest Ridge walks up easy slopes to rock and a chimney; the Southwest Cirque goes up heather gullies. If you have not crossed a gap between glacier and rock, you are not on the west ridge.

The positive landmark above the schrund is a named shape: shelves lead up to a blocky open book — a dihedral corner. That open book is the 5.6 crux and the best-protected pitch on the route. If you cross the schrund and find no open-book corner above you, you have crossed it in the wrong place.

Count the four features in order, because they are all different shapes: schrund, shelves, open book, slab. The slab is taken on its easier left side, not up the middle.

The finish tells you which summit you are under: from below the ridge between the false and main summits, an easy chimney on the left gains the crest. So the route deliberately arrives on the ridge between the two tops — if the chimney you climbed put you straight onto a summit, you are on the false one and the ridge continues.

And if you have to retreat below the summit, the schrund has to work in both directions: a retreat reverses the chimney and slab, downclimbs the open book and re-crosses the schrund. Look at it on the way up with that in mind, because there is no walk-off from this side of the mountain; the walk-off starts at the summit and goes down the South Ridge.
runs: from below the ridge between the false and main summits

text: From Holden Pass, the saddle between Bonanza and Martin at the foot of the West Ridge, head east up the ridge and cut right onto the south side of the ridge into a loose scree gully. Climb the gully and exit via a short Class 3-4 rock step near its top just below an overhang, then keep linking gullies on the south side of the crest up to the summit block. The rock is notoriously loose ("choss"), so a helmet and careful route-finding through the exit moves matter more than raw fitness.

text: Marvin's Ear climbs the skyline ridge of Vega Tower — the sub-summit just east of Vega North Tower/Eros Tower — via a fully bolted 800-ft, 7-pitch alpine sport line (Grade III, 5.10b) through hard metaconglomerate rock. It was the first technical route up Vega Tower's west ridge proper (the only prior technical line, Starshot Ridge 5.8, was established in 1981 on a different aspect); climbing gets progressively more exposed as it skirts over the north face in the upper pitches.

text: This route's crux move is on the ridge itself, not a technical descent: from the ridge crest (reached via the ascent line west of the Prong), drop roughly 70 vertical feet off the crest and wrap around to the south side of McClellan Peak, then scramble up class 3 rock to the true summit. Descend by reversing this exact sequence: downclimb the class 3 south-side rock back to the ~70-ft notch below the ridge crest, regain the crest, and drop back down the steep talus/scree/snow slope west of the Prong to the flat area between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes at ~7,000 ft. From there, rejoin the Snow Lakes Trail (No. 1553) and retrace it past Lake Viviane, the Snow Lakes, and Nada Lake back to the trailhead — summit-to-trailhead typically takes roughly 5–5.5 hours. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required. Watch for loose rock and exposure on the class 3 downclimb (parties have noted going down 20 ft and wrapping to an easier gully when the direct line felt too exposed), ice on the ridge slope in late season, and the same logjam crossing between the Snow Lakes on the way out. Carry an axe/microspikes if snow lingers on the upper slope, since a slip there has real runout consequences.
runs: around to the south side of mcclellan peak
